title: Cotton garter receiving blanket
subtitle: A 90 cm square receiving blanket in DK cotton, for warmer months.
excerpt: A 90 by 90 cm square receiving blanket worked flat in garter stitch using DK cotton. Cotton is cooler than wool and machine-washable without superwash treatment, making it practical for warm-weather newborns. About 320 g of DK cotton.
sourceNotes: Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870), §Cotton Infant Wraps, lists cotton receiving blankets as a summer alternative to wool wraps and notes garter stitch as the recommended fabric for cotton blankets because cotton does not block to shape as readily as wool and garter lies flat without treatment.

knitting.gaugeText: 20 sts × 40 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles (cotton; unblocked).

glossaryTerms.definition: A double-knitting weight yarn spun from cotton fibre. Cotton is heavier than wool at the same thickness, does not stretch as much, and is non-allergenic and machine-washable without special treatment. It knits to a slightly looser stitch gauge than wool DK on the same needles because cotton has less bounce.

content.text: A single-panel square worked flat in garter stitch on 4 mm needles using
DK cotton
, finishing at 90 cm square.

Single-panel construction is ideal for cotton: no seams to check, one piece to launder. Garter stitch was chosen over stocking stitch because cotton does not wet-block as readily as wool, and a cotton blanket in stocking stitch curls at the edges without a border treatment. Garter lies flat in cotton without any blocking. Budget about 320 g (about 640 m / 700 yards) of 100% cotton DK or a cotton-blend DK. Cotton is heavier than wool at the same yardage, so the finished blanket will weigh more than a comparable wool piece. Buy all the yarn in matched dye lots. Cotton dye lots can vary noticeably in depth of tone. Suitable for warm-weather use or for babies with wool sensitivities.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 320 g (about 640 m / 700 yards) of DK-weight cotton or cotton-blend yarn
items.substitutions: 100% cotton DK or cotton-linen blend. Pure linen DK produces a stiffer fabric that softens over many washes. Avoid cotton-acrylic blends that pill quickly.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 100 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

20 stitches and 40 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles using cotton DK. Cotton knits to a slightly different gauge from wool DK on the same needles: cotton has less spring and tends to run looser widthwise. Swatch your chosen yarn for an accurate count. Work a 15 cm square, lay flat without stretching, leave for an hour, and measure the centre 10 cm.

If your gauge is 22 stitches per 10 cm with a 180-stitch cast-on, the blanket will be about 82 cm wide rather than 90 cm. Adjust the cast-on count to reach your target width (multiply 90 by your actual stitch gauge per 10 cm).
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on

Using the long-tail cast-on with cotton DK, cast on 180 stitches. Long-tail tail: (4 × 180) / 10 + 15 = 72 + 15 = 87 cm. Measure 100 cm of tail. Cotton yarn is slightly stiffer than wool and the long-tail cast-on can feel less automatic; work slowly on the cast-on row.
Body

Knit every row until the blanket measures 90 cm from the cast-on edge. At gauge that is 360 rows. When you set this aside between sessions, every row is a knit row so you can resume without any tracking.
Stitch count check-ins
At row 180 (about 45 cm): count across. You should have 180 stitches. At row 358 (about 89.5 cm): count again before the final cast-off.
Common faults
Cotton yarn twisting around the needle: mercerised cotton with a high twist can grip the needle more than wool. Use smooth, tapered needle tips and pull each stitch off cleanly rather than sliding.
Blanket feeling stiff off the needles: cotton softens over the first few washes. A new cotton blanket is stiffer than a wool one but relaxes to a smooth hand after laundering.

Weight of the blanket on the needles causing tension to tighten: cotton is dense and the growing blanket can hang heavy from the needles, pulling the stitches on the left needle tighter than the right. Use a circular needle so the blanket's weight rests in your lap rather than hanging.
Cast-off
Cast off knitwise with a relaxed tension. Cotton cast-offs bind less easily than wool cast-offs because cotton has no spring; work each stitch loose.
Finishing

Weave in both ends with the tapestry needle along garter ridges for at least 5 cm each. Cotton yarn can work loose over time if the ends are woven in too short; weave at least 7 cm and change direction twice.
Care

Machine wash at 40 degrees on a normal cycle; cotton is robust and does not need a delicate cycle unless the yarn is a cotton blend with a delicate fibre component. Tumble dry on a low heat or lay flat. Iron at a medium setting if the blanket appears creased after drying. Cotton blankets can absorb colour from coloured laundry in the same wash; launder with like colours.
What to try next

From a plain cotton garter square, try a striped cotton version with two colours: the same cast-on, garter stitch throughout, alternating every four rows. Cotton takes dye in a matte, flat tone that makes two-colour stripes particularly graphic.
